prompt: In Tufte's sense, what is data ink?

choices.text: Ink that would change if the data changed
choices.why: Right: bars, lines, dots.

choices.text: Any ink printed inside the axes of the chart
choices.why: Gridlines sit inside the axes and are not data ink.

choices.text: The ink used for numbers and labels
choices.why: Labels help read the data; they are not the data's marks.

choices.text: Ink in the colours of the data source's logo
choices.why: Colour choice is unrelated to the idea.

prompt: What does a data-ink ratio of 1 mean?

choices.text: Each mark drawn on the chart shows data
choices.why: Right. In practice nobody gets there, and should not try.

choices.text: Half the ink is data and half is not
choices.why: That would be 0.5.

choices.text: The chart uses one colour for its data, and no other
choices.why: The ratio is about ink, not colours.

choices.text: The chart has exactly one series in it
choices.why: One series can still sit in a lot of junk.

prompt: Tufte's data-___ ratio divides the marks that show data by everything printed on the chart.
A chart uses 80,000 pixels of ink, and 20,000 of them are its bars. What is its data-ink ratio?
Which of these are chartjunk on a bar chart of one series? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The category name beside each bar
choices.why: Without it the bars cannot be read.

choices.text: A shadow behind each bar
choices.why: Right. A second, fainter bar to discount.

choices.text: A grey fill behind the plot area
choices.why: Right. The axes already mark the area.

choices.text: A legend box naming the one colour
choices.why: Right. It names nothing.

choices.text: The unit of the values, in the title
choices.why: A value without a unit is not readable.

prompt: What is wrong with a gradient fill on a bar?

choices.text: It cannot be printed in black and white
choices.why: It can; it is still misleading on screen.

choices.text: It makes the chart file slightly larger
choices.why: Size is not the problem.

choices.text: Gradients are reserved for maps by convention
choices.why: There is no such convention.

choices.text: One end of the bar looks longer than the other
choices.why: Right. A faint end reads as shorter.

prompt: What is the lesson's test for any element on a chart?

choices.text: Does it match the company's colour template?
choices.why: Templates are where much of the junk comes from.

choices.text: Was it drawn by the tool without asking?
choices.why: Some defaults are fine; the question is about the reader.

choices.text: Would the reader miss anything if it went away?
choices.why: Right. If not, delete it; if a little, make it fainter.

choices.text: Does it make the chart look more finished?
choices.why: Looking finished is not information.

prompt: What does matplotlib draw by default that this lesson would usually remove from a bar chart?

choices.text: A grey background behind the bars
choices.why: Its default background is white.

choices.text: A gradient inside each of the bars
choices.why: Its bars are flat by default.

choices.text: A drop shadow under the title
choices.why: It draws no shadows unless asked.

choices.text: A black frame on all four sides
choices.why: Right. Three of those borders carry nothing.

prompt: The cluttered chart had 94,134 pixels of ink, 45,936 of them bars. What is its data-ink ratio, to two decimal places?
The clean chart used 54,780 pixels of ink against the cluttered one's 94,134. How much less ink is that, in percent, to the nearest whole number?
Why did the clean chart have more bar pixels than the cluttered one?

choices.text: The legend box covered part of the longest bar
choices.why: Right. Junk can hide the data, not only surround it.

choices.text: Its bars were drawn in a brighter blue
choices.why: Both used the same colour.

choices.text: The counting program rounded the clean one up
choices.why: Pixels are counted, not rounded.

choices.text: The values written beside the bars count as bar
choices.why: The text is black, far from the bars' blue.

prompt: Put the lesson's decluttering steps in order.
How dark should a gridline be?

choices.text: As dark as the axis, so it lines up
choices.why: Then it competes with the data.

choices.text: As dark as the data, so it can be read
choices.why: The data should be the strongest mark.

choices.text: It depends only on the printer used
choices.why: It depends on the reader's need, on any medium.

choices.text: A faint step away from the background
choices.why: Right. Visible when looked for, invisible otherwise.

prompt: What does `ax.set_axisbelow(True)` do in matplotlib?

choices.text: Moves the axis labels below the chart
choices.why: It changes drawing order, not position.

choices.text: Starts the value axis below zero
choices.why: It does not touch the range.

choices.text: Draws the grid underneath the bars instead of over them
choices.why: Right, so a gridline never crosses the data.

choices.text: Hides the axis for screen readers
choices.why: It is a drawing setting only.

prompt: A line chart of 24 months has month labels along the bottom. Does it need vertical gridlines?

choices.text: Yes, one for every month of the series
choices.why: Twenty-four lines make a mesh.

choices.text: Yes, but only if they are dark
choices.why: Dark gridlines compete with the line.

choices.text: No, a line chart should have no grid
choices.why: Faint horizontal lines are often useful.

choices.text: Rarely: the month labels do that job
choices.why: Right. Horizontal lines help read values; vertical ones repeat the labels.

prompt: What did Bateman and colleagues find in 2010 about heavily illustrated charts?

choices.text: Read far less accurately than plain charts
choices.why: Accuracy was about the same.

choices.text: Forgotten faster than plain charts
choices.why: They were remembered better.

choices.text: Preferred by readers for daily dashboards
choices.why: The study was not about dashboards.

choices.text: Read as accurately, and remembered better later
choices.why: Right. The finding sharpens Tufte's rule rather than overturning it.

prompt: Which removal goes too far?

choices.text: A frame around the plot area
choices.why: The axes already mark the area.

choices.text: The legend of a single series
choices.why: It names nothing.

choices.text: A shadow behind the bars
choices.why: It is a second bar to discount.

choices.text: The category names
choices.why: Right. Without them, six bars mean nothing.

prompt: Which kind of decoration is wrong whatever the chart is for?

choices.text: An illustration on a poster meant to be remembered
choices.why: That can earn its place if it does not distort.

choices.text: Decoration that distorts the data
choices.why: Right: 3D, misleading gradients, pictures that hide values.

choices.text: A faint gridline behind a line chart
choices.why: That is a lookup aid.

choices.text: A title that states the finding
choices.why: Lesson 15 recommends exactly that.

prompt: Find four pieces of chartjunk in this chart.
hint: The shadow peeks out below and right of the longest bar.

prompt: Match each problem to its fix.

pairs.right: say what the bars are in the title

pairs.left: a grid drawn over the bars
three ways to read one value
pairs.right: keep the one the reader needs

prompt: A colleague removes everything from a chart except the bars, to reach the highest data-ink ratio. What is the problem?

choices.text: Bars have a low ratio and lines would do better
choices.why: The ratio does not depend on the chart type like that.

choices.text: The ratio only applies to printed charts
choices.why: It can be measured on screen, as the lesson did.

choices.text: The ratio is a check, not a target
choices.why: Right. Names, units and a title are needed to read it.

choices.text: There is no problem: higher is better
choices.why: A chart without names cannot be read.
